title: [Suite autour de Teichmüller dont] Teichmülleries, 1981-1982 : notes manuscrites (1981-1983, s.d.), lettres (1981, s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
The page finishes item 9 and begins item 10.

(End of 9.) The previous page used the Poincaré homology sphere S^3/Γ, with Γ the binary icosahedral group of order 120, and the Edwards–Cannon double suspension theorem. The point was that a cone over a compact manifold S can be a (topological) manifold without S being a sphere. Grothendieck concludes that, to state conditions on a conically stratified space that force links to be spheres, one should (following Deligne) work in a framework such as PL, or a better one 'à la Thurston' (geometric structures). The purely topological category is unsuited to this. He then claims, with the marginal note 'à vérifier avec soin', that for locally finite regular 'cartes' (higher-dimensional regular maps, i.e. regular cell complexes) these difficulties disappear. The reason is that everything is combinatorial and flag-transitive, so links are again regular cartes of lower rank.

(10.) He asks whether the groups occurring as automorphism groups of simply connected (locally finite?) regular cartes are all Coxeter groups. In modern terms these would be string Coxeter groups, with a linear diagram and Schläfli symbol {p,q,...,r}.
- The finite ones are classified in Bourbaki, Lie ch. IV–VI.
- They seem to correspond to spheres carrying the evident 'simplicial' cell decomposition, namely the Coxeter complex, i.e. the barycentric subdivision of the boundary of the regular polytope.
- Deligne's expectation is that all simply connected regular cartes, finite or infinite, appear in Bourbaki, at least in the nonsingular case. These are the spherical, affine (Euclidean) and, as the next page says, hyperbolic tessellations. The hyperbolic case is cut out by an invariant quadratic form of Lorentzian signature, on one sheet of the hyperboloid, using traces of the simplicial cones (fundamental domains).

In modern language: a regular polytope whose facets and vertex figures are spherical (nonsingular), and whose flag complex is simply connected, is the universal polytope {p,...,r}. Its automorphism group is the string Coxeter group. All its proper parabolic subgroups are finite, so the group is spherical, affine, or compact hyperbolic (Lannér). This is precisely the regular polytopes and honeycombs of Coxeter's list (including hyperbolic {5,3,5}, {4,3,5}, {3,5,3}, {5,3,3,3}, ...). The page serves the 'Teichmülleries' programme of combinatorial maps/dessins and their higher-dimensional analogues.
errors: Without the 'nonsingular' / local sphericity hypothesis on facets and vertex figures, the question as first posed fails. Topologically simply connected regular polytopes need not be universal. If facets or vertex figures are themselves non-universal (e.g. hemi-polytope facets), the automorphism group is a proper quotient of a Coxeter group (a string C-group). Grothendieck's later restriction to 'cas sans singularités' (next page) is needed.

'Finite ones correspond to spheres' is right for the universal ones (the Coxeter complex of a finite Coxeter group is a sphere). Finite regular cartes in general, e.g. projective or toroidal regular maps, are not spheres. These are excluded by the simple connectivity hypothesis.

The claim that the PL-type difficulties disappear for locally finite regular cartes is left unverified (flagged by the margin note). It is true, essentially, because links are again regular cartes and induction applies, but it is not proved here.

ideas.what: Topological category inadequate for characterizing conical stratified spaces whose links must be spheres; use PL or geometric (Thurston-type) structures instead

missed.claim: Grothendieck and Deligne independently frame the characterization of universal regular polytopes as Coxeter groups via simple connectivity of the cell complex. This is the same insight as Tits's contemporaneous local-approach theorem and anticipates McMullen–Schulte's universal polytopes, which the polytope literature attributes elsewhere. It is largely known, so it serves only as historical context.
missed.quote: Les groupes apparaissant comme groupes d'automorphismes de "cartes" régulières simplement connexes (loc. finies?), ne sont-ils pas tous des groupes de Coxeter.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Documents Deligne's and Grothendieck's 1981 involvement with regular-polytope/Coxeter classification, linked to the dessins programme. It has historical rather than mathematical novelty.

deep.surprise_reason: The mathematics, Coxeter groups as automorphism groups of universal regular polytopes and the spherical/affine/hyperbolic trichotomy, is classical (Coxeter, Tits, Lannér). The page is of historical interest only, for Deligne's remark and its link with the Esquisse.
